editorial.summary: Episode 74 is the clearest early DVDASA record of a production recognizing that contextual anonymity failed. During the show, the young guest from Episodes 70–71 reports that she has been identified and asks for both YouTube appearances removed because the exposure is starting to ruin her life. Participants immediately say the videos should come down and that the situation could destroy her life, while others argue that she signed a waiver, knew the premise and never used her real name. Those defenses fail on the episode's own facts: her face and contextual clues enabled recognition. Audio is not automatically safe merely because the image is removed. Later, Bobby Lee asks to protect an absent friend's name after another participant reveals something, and the room invents a one-pass redaction rule. The map preserves the governance fight but withholds the person, employer, relationship and claim. Radical honesty covers one's own life; it does not convert other people's health, sex, employment or relationship information into a host-owned asset. A separate staged sex-position demonstration proceeds after an audible no and includes exposed-genital contact. The room later calls it workplace harassment, molestation and the beginning of rape. Adult-entertainment work, initial participation, lack of resistance, later laughter, claimed non-arousal and retrospective approval do not retroactively supply consent. The episode also supplies useful creator history—Slink Johnson's reported opportunity, Bobby Lee's discovery of Choe through a Vice DVD and signed plush, DVDASA's alternate BOBASA name, party planning, comedy networks and show analytics—while correcting medical, historical, racial, disaster and cultural references.
